parts.meaning: to shade (from nue, cloud, Latin nubes)

nuance.path: French nuer meant to shade colors gradually into each other, from nue, cloud, the way cloud colors blend. Nuance kept that sense of a fine gradation, a subtle shade of difference in meaning.

nullify.path: Latin nullus (none) combined with facere (to make) gives nullify: to make something count as nothing, voiding its legal force.

numinous.path: Latin numen named the divine power or will, imagined as a god's nod of assent. Numinous describes anything that carries that felt sense of a hidden divine presence.

obdurate.path: Latin durus meant hard; obdurare, intensified with ob-, meant to harden completely. Obdurate describes someone hardened against persuasion, stubbornly refusing to change.

obeisance.path: Latin oboedire, to obey, literally meant to listen or hearken toward someone. Obeisance kept the sense of a gesture, like a bow, showing that submissive, respectful hearing.

obfuscate.path: Latin fuscus meant dark or dusky; obfuscare, to darken over, described casting something into shadow. Obfuscate kept that image: to deliberately darken understanding, making something unclear.

objective.path: Latin obicere meant to throw something in front of, to present it as an object. Objective describes something existing out there as a presented fact, independent of the observer's personal feelings.

parts.meaning: to quarrel, dispute at law (ius, law)

objurgate.path: Latin jurgare meant to quarrel or argue, often in a legal sense; adding ob- (against) gives objurgare, to scold sharply. English objurgate kept the sense of a severe, formal rebuke.

obliging.path: Latin obligare meant to bind someone by a duty or favor. Obliging describes someone eager to bind themselves to helping others, willingly doing favors.

oblique.path: Latin obliquus described a slanting, indirect angle, neither straight nor level. Oblique extended that spatial sense to indirect, evasive speech or approach that doesn't go straight at its point.

oblivious.path: Latin oblivisci meant to forget, possibly picturing memory being smoothed or wiped away like writing on a wax tablet. Oblivious describes someone whose awareness has been wiped clean, completely unaware.

obloquy.path: Latin loqui, to speak, combined with ob- (against) gives obloquium, speech directed against someone. Obloquy kept that sense: harsh, condemning public speech aimed at a person's reputation.

obscure.path: Latin obscurus meant dark or covered in shadow. The verb obscure kept that sense: to cover something over so it can't be clearly seen or understood.

obsequious.path: Latin sequi, to follow, combined with ob- (toward) gives obsequi, to comply by following someone's wishes. Obsequious sharpened that: following and pleasing someone to an excessive, fawning degree.

parts.meaning: to fall into disuse (solere, to be accustomed)

obsolete.path: Latin obsolescere meant to fall into disuse, to wear out from lack of habitual use. Obsolete describes something that has worn out of common use, no longer useful.

obstinate.path: Latin obstinare meant to stand firm, to persist in a position. Obstinate kept that image: someone standing their ground, stubbornly refusing to change course.

obstreperous.path: Latin strepere, to make noise, combined with ob- (against) gives obstrepere, to clamor loudly against something. Obstreperous kept that sense: noisily and stubbornly resisting control.

obstructionist.path: Latin struere, to build, combined with ob- (against) gives obstruere, to block by building in the way. An obstructionist deliberately piles up obstacles to block progress.

obtain.path: Latin tenere, to hold, combined with ob- (intensive) gives obtinere, to hold firmly, to gain possession. English obtain kept the sense of acquiring, and a secondary sense of a rule holding in force.

obtrude.path: Latin trudere, to thrust or push, combined with ob- (toward) gives obtrudere, to push something forcibly at someone. Obtrude kept that sense: to impose oneself where unwelcome.

obtuse.path: Latin tundere, to beat or pound, combined with ob- (against) gives obtundere, to blunt something by repeated beating. Obtuse first described a blunt angle, then a mind that is blunt, slow to understand.

obviate.literal: to come in the way of
obviate.path: Latin ob via, literally in the way, gave obviare, to block something by getting in its path before it arrives. Obviate kept that sense: to head off a problem in advance, removing the need to deal with it.

occlude.path: Latin claudere, to close, combined with the intensive ob- gives occludere, to shut something up entirely. Occlude kept that sense: to block or obstruct a passage completely.

occult.path: Latin occulere, to hide completely, built from ob- (over) and a root meaning to cover or conceal. Occult describes what's deliberately hidden from ordinary knowledge, associated with secret or supernatural practices.

odious.path: Latin odium meant hatred; odiosus described anything that provokes it. English odious kept that sense: extremely unpleasant, repulsive enough to be hated.

odium.path: Latin odium named hatred or intense dislike directly. English kept it whole: widespread hatred or disgust directed at someone.

offhand.path: A native English compound picturing something done straight off the hand, without setup or forethought, hence casual and unprepared.

parts.meaning: duty, service (opus, work + facere, to do)

officious.path: Latin officium meant duty or service; officiosus originally meant dutifully helpful. The sense soured in English: officious now means meddling with unwanted, self-important helpfulness.

offset.path: A native compound: to set something off against something else so the two balance out, one counteracting the other.

olfactory.path: Latin olere, to smell, combined with facere (to do) gives olfacere, to perceive by smell. Olfactory simply means relating to the sense of smell.

ominous.path: Latin omen named a sign taken to foretell the future, often an ill one. Ominous describes anything that carries such a sign, suggesting bad things to come.

omnipresent.path: Latin omnis (all) combined with present names something existing at all places simultaneously, a term originally used of God's presence in theology.

omniscience.path: Latin omnis (all) plus scientia (knowledge) names the state of knowing everything, a quality classically attributed to God.

omniscient.path: The adjective form of omniscience (see omniscience): knowing everything.

onerous.path: Latin onus meant a load or burden; onerosus described anything weighed down by one. Onerous kept that sense: involving a heavy, oppressive burden of duty or work.

onset.path: A native compound originally meaning an attack, a setting on an enemy. It broadened to the beginning of anything, especially something unwelcome like an illness or storm.

opaque.path: Latin opacus described something cast in shadow, blocking light. Opaque kept that sense of blocking light and extended it to ideas or writing too dark to see through clearly.

opine.path: Latin opinari meant to suppose or hold a belief, the root of opinion. Opine kept that direct sense: to state a view, often with a hint that it's unsolicited.

opportunism.path: Latin opportunus described a wind blowing favorably toward the harbor, hence convenient timing. Opportunism took that idea and gave it a negative twist: seizing advantage from circumstances without regard to principle.

oppress.path: Latin premere, to press, combined with ob- (against) gives opprimere, to press down on, to crush. Oppress kept that sense: to keep people down through the crushing weight of unjust force.

opprobrium.path: Latin probrum meant a shameful or reproachful act; combined with ob- (against), opprobrium named the disgrace hurled at someone for it. English kept the sense of harsh public condemnation.

optimal.path: Latin optimus was the superlative form of good, meaning best. Optimal simply describes the best possible option given the circumstances.

optimum.path: Borrowed directly from Latin optimum, the neuter of optimus, best: the most favorable condition or amount.

opulence.path: Latin ops meant power or wealth, resources at one's disposal. Opulentus described someone overflowing with such riches. Opulence kept that sense of lavish, ostentatious wealth.

opulent.path: The adjective form of opulence (see opulence): luxurious and richly appointed, overflowing with wealth.

oration.path: Latin orare, to speak or plead, traces to os, mouth. Oratio named the act of formal speaking. English oration kept that sense: a formal, often ceremonial speech.

oratorio.path: Named after the Italian oratorio, a chapel for prayer (from Latin orare, to pray) where Philip Neri's followers staged musical devotions in the 16th century. Oratorio came to mean the large-scale sacred musical works performed there.

ordain.path: Latin ordinare meant to arrange things in their proper order or rank. Ordain kept that in two directions: to officially decree something into law, and to formally induct someone into a proper rank or office.

ornate.path: Latin ornare meant to decorate or equip something splendidly. Ornate kept that direct sense: elaborately, often excessively, decorated.

ornery.path: Ornery began as a slurred American pronunciation of ordinary, first meaning plain or of common, low quality. The sense soured further into bad-tempered and stubbornly difficult.
